Has anyone here tips or input on the subject of writing protagonists of a gender other than one's own?

This is a topic that fascinates me quite a bit, and I hope that maybe someone else here shares this interest. Thank you in advance.

This topic interests me as well!

I suggest listening to people of the required gender actually speaking, specifically in everyday life. Ideally these people would be as close a match to your intended character as possible (age group, social class, etc - a good character profile is therefore important). Listen to them speaking one-to-one and in groups; speaking to someone of the same gender, but also of the opposite gender - and in mixed-gender groups if you really want to do a thorough job.

When you listen, men and women do speak and behave differently, depending on what number and gender they are communicating with. For example, it's easy to tell when your friend has a man or a woman on the other end of their phone call, and if it's a parent or a grandparent!

The reason why I suggest specifically everyday life situations for your gender research is because I believe that these will provide necessarily raw, unprocessed material that will absorb your writing style as you process it into a written piece. If you research too much based upon, for example, other authors' written pieces then you will be absorbing too much of their personal style and missing the essence of the ideal raw material (everyday life scenarios). The same applies to researching based upon films: you will be getting a pre-scripted character there, so not ideal. Perhaps documentaries would be a convenient alternative - or anything candid and unscripted.

Title says it all, I think. Which strategies do you employ in order to make characters immediately recognizable by their voice?
On making characters sound different from each other

I think that an important step towards achieving this is to know your characters very well before you begin writing, so that means developing a detailed character profile for each character at the planning stage. Once you know every aspect of your character's background and personality then you will know how he/she will speak.

I suppose that might be stating the obvious, but I think that this approach allows you to choose a set of key differentiating characteristics for each character in advance, which then enables you to apply those consistently throughout your story.

With the fine-tuning and differentiation of characteristics carried out in advance, you can create 'space' between each character, where 'space' in this sense means that there is no overlap of dialogue characteristics that may confuse the reader.
